title: ABG and VBG
subtitle: Acid–base status, ventilation, oxygenation and lactate
summary: Acid–base status, ventilation, oxygenation and lactate
introduction: Use the analyser and local laboratory ranges. A VBG can support assessment of pH, bicarbonate and trends in carbon dioxide, but venous pO₂ must not be used to assess oxygenation. Record the oxygen device and flow or FiO₂ at the time of sampling.

rows.name: pH
notes: VBG pH is normally slightly lower than arterial pH.

rows.name: pCO₂
lowInterpretation: Supports respiratory alkalosis or respiratory compensation when interpreted with pH and bicarbonate.
highInterpretation: Supports respiratory acidosis or respiratory compensation when interpreted with pH and bicarbonate.
notes: PvCO₂ is normally slightly higher than arterial pCO₂.

rows.name: Bicarbonate
lowInterpretation: Supports metabolic acidosis or renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis.
highInterpretation: Supports metabolic alkalosis or renal compensation for respiratory acidosis.

rows.name: Base excess
rows.referenceRange: RVH arterial blood-gas reference: −2.5 to +2.5 mmol/L
lowInterpretation: A negative value supports a metabolic acid load.
highInterpretation: A positive value supports metabolic alkalosis or chronic compensation.

rows.name: pO₂
lowInterpretation: PaO₂ below 8.0 kPa suggests hypoxaemic respiratory failure; confirm inspired oxygen and SpO₂.
notes: Do not use venous pO₂ to assess arterial oxygenation.

rows.name: Lactate
highInterpretation: 2.0–3.9 mmol/L is abnormal; at least 4.0 mmol/L is a major abnormality requiring urgent assessment of the cause.
notes: A normal lactate does not exclude sepsis, shock or another serious illness.

rows.name: Respiratory acidosis
notes: Consider hypoventilation, COPD/asthma fatigue, sedative/opioid effect, neuromuscular weakness or severe obesity hypoventilation. Raised bicarbonate may indicate chronic compensation or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis.

rows.name: Metabolic acidosis
notes: Consider lactate, ketones, renal failure, diarrhoea, toxins and the anion gap. Low pCO₂ may indicate respiratory compensation.

rows.name: Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis
rows.referenceRange: Low pH with raised pCO₂ and low bicarbonate

rows.name: Respiratory alkalosis
notes: Consider pain/anxiety only after excluding hypoxia, PE, sepsis, pregnancy, liver disease and salicylates.

rows.name: Metabolic alkalosis
notes: Consider vomiting, gastric losses, diuretics, hypokalaemia, mineralocorticoid excess or alkali administration.

rows.name: Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis
rows.referenceRange: High pH with low pCO₂ and raised bicarbonate
notes: Both low pCO₂ and raised bicarbonate are driving the pH up.

calculations.title: Basic acid–base pattern
calculations.formula: rule-based interpretation of pH, pCO2 and bicarbonate
interpretation: This is a basic pattern recognition aid and does not calculate expected compensation.
Review base excess, anion gap, sample quality and the clinical picture; consider mixed disorders.

inputs.label: pH
inputs.validationMessage: Enter a plausible blood pH between 6.0 and 8.0.

urgentFindings: pH below 7.25 or a falling pH.
pH below 7.35 with raised pCO₂ and drowsiness or exhaustion.
PaO₂ below the expected range despite oxygen.
overrides: Escalate based on the patient and trajectory rather than a single threshold.
Always review potassium, glucose, ketones, lactate, haemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin/methemoglobin when clinically relevant.

commonPatterns.title: Acute hypoventilation / respiratory acidosis
findings: Bicarbonate normal or only mildly raised (little time for renal compensation)
Drowsiness, exhaustion, opioid/sedative exposure or severe airway obstruction
interpretation: Suggests acute hypoventilation from causes such as opioid/sedative effect, neuromuscular weakness, severe asthma/COPD exacerbation with fatigue, or upper airway obstruction
A normal-range bicarbonate with acidaemia suggests this is acute rather than an acute-on-chronic picture
actions: Treat as time-critical if pH is below 7.35 with drowsiness or exhaustion (see urgent findings)
Identify and treat the cause of hypoventilation (reverse sedation/opioid where appropriate, treat bronchospasm, support the airway)
Reassess ventilation and repeat gas after any intervention rather than relying on a single result

commonPatterns.title: Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis
findings: Known COPD or chronic respiratory disease
interpretation: A raised bicarbonate indicates renal compensation has had time to develop, suggesting a chronic respiratory acidosis that has now acutely decompensated rather than a purely acute event
The patient's own baseline gas (if known) is valuable context — a pH within their usual compensated range may be less concerning than the same pH would be in someone without chronic disease
actions: Compare with any previous blood gas results to establish the patient's own baseline where available
Treat as time-critical if pH is below 7.35 with drowsiness/exhaustion, or if pH is below 7.25 regardless of chronicity (see urgent findings)
Record the oxygen device and flow/FiO₂ carefully — controlled oxygen therapy is often relevant in this group

commonPatterns.title: Likely high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
findings: Raised lactate, ketones, or known renal failure/toxin exposure
interpretation: Consider the standard high-anion-gap causes: lactate (hypoperfusion, sepsis, seizure, metformin), ketones (DKA, starvation, alcoholic ketoacidosis), renal failure (uraemia), and toxins (salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol)
The specific cause changes management significantly, so the pattern alone is only a starting point
actions: Check lactate and ketones as the two most common and rapidly actionable causes (see further testing)
Consider toxin ingestion and an osmolal gap if the cause is not clear from lactate/ketones/renal function
Treat as time-critical for pH <7.25, a falling pH, or a mixed acidosis pattern (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis
findings: Low pH with raised pCO₂ and low bicarbonate
interpretation: Both respiratory and metabolic processes are driving the pH down simultaneously with no compensation evident — this is a high-risk pattern and often indicates a severely unwell patient (for example combined respiratory failure and shock/sepsis)
actions: Treat as time-critical regardless of the specific underlying cause (see urgent findings)
Request lactate, ketones, U&E and consider toxin screening to identify the metabolic component while addressing ventilation
Arrange urgent senior/medical review — this pattern usually needs simultaneous respiratory and circulatory support

commonPatterns.title: Respiratory alkalosis — exclude a serious cause first
interpretation: Pain and anxiety are common causes but are diagnoses of exclusion — hypoxia, PE, sepsis, pregnancy, liver disease and salicylate poisoning can all present with a respiratory alkalosis and must be actively considered first
actions: Check oxygenation directly (SpO₂, PaO₂ on an arterial sample if oxygenation assessment is needed) rather than assuming a benign cause
Consider PE risk factors, sepsis features, pregnancy status and salicylate exposure before attributing the picture to pain/anxiety
Request lactate and consider further targeted testing based on the differential being excluded (see further testing)

commonPatterns.title: Metabolic alkalosis — GI loss or diuretic picture
findings: Vomiting, gastric losses, diuretic use, or low potassium
interpretation: Vomiting/gastric losses and diuretics are the most common causes; hypokalaemia both results from and perpetuates this pattern, and mineralocorticoid excess or alkali administration are less common alternatives
actions: Request U&E to check potassium, which is often low and needs correction alongside the underlying cause (see further testing)
Review diuretic use and ask about vomiting/gastric losses (e.g. nasogastric drainage, pyloric stenosis)
Arrange medical review if the cause is not clear or the alkalosis is marked

commonPatterns.title: Raised lactate on the gas
findings: Hypotension, tachycardia, mottled skin or signs of infection
interpretation: Supports hypoperfusion or sepsis and is an important severity marker, but a normal lactate does not exclude sepsis or shock, and a raised lactate can also reflect seizure, severe work of breathing, beta-agonist use, liver dysfunction, metformin accumulation or toxins
actions: Treat as time-critical if lactate is ≥4.0 mmol/L or the patient shows signs of shock (see urgent findings)
Consider non-hypoperfusion causes if the clinical picture does not fit sepsis/shock
Repeat the gas to assess lactate trend and response to treatment

rationale: Potassium is essential context for acid–base disturbance (both cause and consequence), and renal function helps identify uraemic or renal causes of metabolic acidosis
Identifies ketoacidosis (diabetic, alcoholic or starvation) as the cause of a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Needed alongside ketones and pH to identify and grade DKA/HHS when a metabolic acidosis or hyperosmolar picture is present

furtherTesting.test: Pulse oximetry / arterial sample for oxygenation
rationale: Venous pO₂ cannot be used to assess oxygenation; an arterial sample or reliable SpO₂ is needed whenever hypoxaemia is a concern
Supports identification of toxic alcohol ingestion when a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis is not explained by lactate, ketones or renal failure
Acid–base status can change rapidly with treatment or deterioration; trend is often more useful than a single value, particularly after an intervention

specimens.notes: Heparinised blood-gas syringe. Fill to the correct volume (1 mL or 3 mL), exclude air, cap and send immediately. Analyse within 30 minutes; do not send via pneumatic chute or on ice.
